body.text: On the evening of November 20, in Türkiye’s Mediterranean beach city of Antalya, journalists began packing their laptops, dismantling television equipment, and preparing to leave the venue of the United Nations climate summit. Behind closed doors, negotiators from nearly 200 countries were still arguing over the wording of the summit’s final political text.

The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) was scheduled to end that Friday. The media centre, which had accommodated thousands of journalists during the fortnight, was gradually emptying. Camera crews prepared their final transmissions, and delegates checked flights and hotel bookings. There was still no final declaration to report.

Outside, Antalya went about its day. Trams ran through the city, and tourists walked the cobbled streets of the historic Kaleiçi quarter, with the old harbour beyond. Inside, diplomats were struggling to agree on a response to a crisis that threatens coastlines, livelihoods, and entire nations.

By Saturday, November 21, the talks had run past their scheduled close. Several ministers and delegates had left, and others had flights booked and could not stay indefinitely. The possibility of continuing the discussions over Zoom was being considered, though the conference had brought tens of thousands of people to Türkiye.

On Sunday, November 22, the second day of overtime, the answer came. The summit would conclude without consensus on its central political declaration. In the Anatolian Hall of the EXPO 2016 Antalya complex, Turkish Environment Minister and COP31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that the proposed Antalya Pact had failed to secure agreement. “There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” Kurum told delegates. “Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision and we will respect their decision.”

The European Union, Panama, Norway, and several climate-vulnerable island nations had rejected a draft that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, the principal source of the greenhouse gases driving global warming. Panama’s representative told the closing session: “The atmosphere does not negotiate, science does not negotiate, and the planet cannot wait any longer.”

Antalya, situated between the Mediterranean Sea and the Taurus Mountains, is better known for its beaches, resorts, ancient ruins, and historic neighbourhoods than for international diplomacy. It draws millions of visitors a year.

During COP31, the city took on a different character. Delegates wearing accreditation badges filled hotel lobbies, restaurants, and public transport, and conversations about emissions, renewable energy, and climate finance could be overheard in cafés and tram carriages.

Accredited delegates and journalists could ride the trams free of charge, and transport links connected the conference site with the wider city. Passengers moved between modern residential neighbourhoods, shopping districts, and historic areas. The older tram line passed close to Kaleiçi, where narrow streets run between restored Ottoman houses, souvenir shops, and restaurants serving Turkish and Mediterranean food. The old harbour, with its fishing boats and tourist vessels, recalled the city’s maritime history.

The Mediterranean region is a recognised climate hotspot, with rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, forest fires, and increasing pressure on water resources. Türkiye has itself had large wildfires along its Mediterranean coast.

Security checkpoints, accreditation counters, exhibition pavilions, meeting halls, restaurants, and media workspaces occupied a large area of the conference venue. Television crews looked for places to broadcast live, and reporters moved between press conferences and closed-door briefings.

Türkiye put considerable effort into presenting itself as a capable host. Exhibition halls displayed renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles, waste-management systems, and water-conservation methods. A zero-waste pavilion showed how recycling, efficient resource use, and changes in consumption could reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Elsewhere, scientists and entrepreneurs presented technologies for recovering valuable materials from discarded solar panels and batteries. Ashish Khanna, director general of the International Solar Alliance, said recycling solar panels and batteries could create investment opportunities of nearly $15 billion over five years.

Another presentation focussed on communicating climate risks. Shen Xiaomeng, head of the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, argued that scientific warnings often fail because they do not describe danger in terms ordinary people understand. “We’re not lacking knowledge,” she said. “What we are lacking is to distill the knowledge and translate it into messages.”
In the public Green Zone, companies and scientists presented technologies. In the Blue Zone, the UN-run area for accredited participants, governments disagreed over who would pay to deploy them.
Agenda and drafts

COP31 opened on November 9 with Türkiye holding the presidency and Australia leading the negotiations. The arrangement was a diplomatic compromise between two countries with different energy systems and regional interests. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan addressed the Leaders’ Summit on November 11, linking climate action to development, international cooperation, and the responsibilities of governments. About 100 leaders and senior representatives took part. The presidencies called it an “implementation COP”, focussed on turning earlier commitments into measurable action.

Türkiye promoted an initiative known as “35 by 35”, which seeks to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. It envisaged replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with electric transport, expanding electric heating, and encouraging industries to adopt electrical technologies.

Environmental organisations noted that electrification does not by itself cut emissions: if the extra electricity comes from coal or gas, the benefit is much smaller. They demanded that electrification targets be explicitly linked to renewable energy and a reduction in fossil fuel use.

Simon Bradshaw of Greenpeace Australia Pacific raised the point early in the negotiations. “The flagship electrification pledge is of course in there,” he told reporters, but it was not sufficiently linked to the need to remove fossil fuels from energy systems.

The first major negotiating draft, released on November 16, ran to 144 paragraphs. It was a compilation of parties’ proposals, not an agreed text, and it included competing formulations on transitioning away from fossil fuels. It also proposed raising annual adaptation finance for developing countries to $120 billion by 2035.
A slimmed-down draft published on November 19 removed explicit references to transitioning away from coal, oil, and natural gas, along with the $120 billion adaptation finance figure.

Environmental organisations and climate-vulnerable countries said the changes reversed commitments that had taken decades to secure. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, governments had agreed for the first time in a global climate decision to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. The Antalya draft, critics said, fell short of that. “This new text has gone backwards from the one released earlier in the week,” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said. “If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”

Turkish officials rejected the criticism. “I do not think we are taking a step back,” Kurum told reporters. He argued that governments needed to implement commitments already made rather than repeatedly reopening earlier negotiations.

Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen also stressed electrification and the need to confront the prospect of global temperatures exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold. “There’s always a fossil fuel discussion at all the COPs I’ve been at,” Bowen told journalists.

Critics argued that a programme centred on electrification and carbon capture, without a clear commitment to reduce fossil fuel dependence, could leave existing energy systems largely unchanged. Tzeporah Berman, chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, criticised the reluctance to address fossil fuel production directly. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it,” she said. “They’re literally pouring gas on the fire.”

The dispute concerned the future of the fossil fuel industries, the economic survival of petroleum-producing countries, the development ambitions of poorer nations, and the responsibilities of wealthy countries whose historical emissions caused much of the present crisis.
The closing plenary

Frustration surfaced during a late-night plenary session on Friday, when a climate activist interrupted proceedings, holding a red noose around his neck. “You are killing the future. You are killing the future. Why don’t you just kill me now?” he shouted. Security personnel escorted him from the hall, but he continued to denounce the removal of fossil fuel language and the weakening of adaptation finance commitments. “The Global South can’t wait for this, and yet you just keep doing nothing,” he said.

Protests were not confined to the official venue. Across Antalya, the People’s Climate Summit brought together environmental organisations, grassroots campaigners, and representatives of communities affected by environmental destruction. Discussions there went beyond emissions targets to the political and economic structures that participants held responsible for environmental damage.

The war in Gaza also featured in these gatherings. Campaigners pointed to its environmental consequences, including damaged water and sanitation systems, destroyed agricultural land, and the large reconstruction needs facing Palestinians.
Some environmental organisations complained of accreditation barriers and restrictions on participation, while governments and corporate representatives had extensive access.

The presence of fossil fuel industry representatives was another source of controversy. According to research cited by environmental campaigners, about 700 carbon capture and storage lobbyists had access to COP31, compared with 531 the previous year. Larissa Baldwin, co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change, accused the organisers of failing to provide adequate leadership.

Over the preceding days, Kurum and Bowen had tried to reconcile conflicting positions through consultations with individual delegations, looking for language that would satisfy governments demanding stronger climate action without alienating major fossil fuel producers. The Antalya Pact was the result.

When the final text came before the plenary, several delegations objected. Ireland’s Climate and Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the European Union, rejected the document because it did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
Panama, Vanuatu, the Marshall Islands, Norway, and Belize also objected. Vanuatu warned that limiting warming to 1.5°C was a question of survival.

Other countries were prepared to accept the document despite its weaknesses. Pakistan, Syria, and Venezuela supported its adoption. Venezuela’s representative argued that the proposed decision deserved to carry Antalya’s name. Egypt acknowledged shortcomings on climate finance and trade but urged countries not to let mutual accusations destroy the negotiating process.

The positions did not follow a simple divide between rich and poor countries. Some developing nations preferred a weak agreement to none. Others feared that accepting an inadequate text would legitimise a retreat from earlier commitments.

Russia supported avoiding explicit language on fossil fuels, while Saudi Arabia and other petroleum-producing countries resisted proposals that could constrain their energy industries. The European Union pressed for stronger language, despite continuing tensions over the scale and predictability of finance from wealthy countries.

Kurum acknowledged the impasse. “No one got everything they wanted,” he told delegates, appealing for compromise. When objections continued, he said consensus was absent: “There are parties in the hall who oppose this text; we see that there is no agreement on this text.”

Climate finance was the second major point of dispute. Developing countries have consistently argued that wealthy industrialised nations bear a special responsibility for financing climate action. Adaptation funding pays for measures such as flood defences, drought-resistant agriculture, water conservation, and infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather. The removal of the $120 billion annual target angered African countries and other vulnerable nations.

Ghana’s Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, speaking as ministerial chair of the African Group of Negotiators, rejected the idea that developing countries should settle for declarations unsupported by resources. “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them,” she said. “We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people.”

The UN Environment Programme estimates that developing countries will need about $305 billion a year for adaptation by 2035. New pledges to the Adaptation Fund at COP31 totalled about $50.2 million, against an annual fundraising target of $300 million.

Spain made the largest pledge, about $27.8 million, followed by Germany with $11.1 million, and Ireland with $6.7 million. Several wealthy countries, including the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Italy, and Australia, made no new pledges to the fund.

Kenya’s representative criticised the lack of concrete figures and initial milestones for increasing adaptation support. Iran also stressed the obligation of developed countries to provide finance and transfer technology.
India’s position

India’s stance at COP31 followed its long-standing defence of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Under it, all countries must address climate change, but their obligations should reflect historical emissions, development levels, and national circumstances.

India argues that wealthy countries should cut emissions faster while providing finance and technology to developing nations. It also says millions of people still need affordable energy, jobs, housing, and industrial development. Its per capita emissions remain well below those of many developed economies, although its total emissions are among the world’s highest.

At Antalya, India and the Like-Minded Developing Countries resisted uniform electrification targets that lacked guaranteed finance and flexibility for national circumstances. The proposed “35 by 35” target raised questions about who would pay for the infrastructure, electricity networks, industrial changes, and technology upgrades. For countries with limited resources, electrification involves far more than replacing one energy source with another.

India is also among the countries most vulnerable to climate change. Extreme heat, erratic monsoons, flooding, water scarcity, and agricultural disruption threaten millions of Indians. Environmental change in the Himalaya affects glaciers, rivers, and downstream populations, and air pollution in cities adds to the human cost of fossil fuel use.

India withdrew its offer to host COP33 in 2028 before the Antalya summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi had proposed hosting the conference at COP28 in Dubai in December 2023, and the announcement was presented at the time as evidence of India’s growing international stature and its ambition to lead the developing world on climate.

In April 2026, India told the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change that it would no longer pursue hosting. Reports said the letter cited a review of its commitments for 2028 and gave no further detail. Experts cited by Mongabay India linked the decision to shifting climate and geopolitical priorities.

COP33 is expected to oversee the second Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement. The stocktake evaluates collective progress towards the agreement’s temperature goals and is intended to encourage stronger national climate commitments. As host and president, India would have been expected to facilitate ambitious outcomes while holding to its own positions on energy security, finance, and development. Mongabay India reported that hosting in the stocktake year would have added pressure to push for stronger ambition.

Türkiye provided the facilities and led intensive diplomacy, yet the summit ended without agreement, and the presidency’s handling of the texts drew criticism from several delegations and campaigners.
Earlier crises

Antalya was not the first time a United Nations climate conference ended without agreement on its principal negotiating objectives. An earlier collapse came at COP6 in The Hague, Netherlands, in November 2000, amid disagreements over implementing the Kyoto Protocol, particularly the rules on carbon sinks, emissions trading, and the obligations of industrialised countries. Negotiations were suspended and resumed in Bonn, Germany, in July 2001, where governments reached a political agreement.

COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 ended with governments only taking note of the Copenhagen Accord instead of adopting it by consensus. At Antalya, the conference failed to adopt a central political declaration, even though governments had agreed in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels.

Peru’s representative, speaking for the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean, questioned how the negotiations were run. The representative criticised the circulation of important texts in the early hours, which left delegations little time to examine them. “We are not proposing these because we are against the principle of consensus,” the representative said while discussing possible changes to decision-making procedures. “We are proposing them so that consensus can once again produce results.”
The intervention touched on a long-running debate over whether consensus, a rule meant to protect weaker countries, can also produce paralysis.

Not every initiative announced at COP31 depended on the pact. Türkiye used the conference to promote renewable energy investment, electrification, and environmental technologies. Business agreements and investment plans worth more than $26 billion were reported during the summit, including projects in renewable energy, nuclear power studies, and international financial institutions.

Li Shuo, a veteran observer of Chinese climate policy who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said hosting a COP offered an exceptional opportunity to attract investment. Environmental groups said commercial agreements cannot replace political commitments, and that carbon capture, whose costs and effectiveness vary widely, should not become a reason to keep expanding fossil fuel production.

Amnesty International argued that rejecting an inadequate agreement was preferable to accepting a document that could undermine climate justice. “Rejecting the dangerous ‘cover decision’ text was an important act of resistance,” said Ann Harrison, the organisation’s climate justice policy adviser. She also described the overall outcome as a major failure.
The United States sent no official delegation, following the Trump administration’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

As the summit ended, Antalya was returning to its usual rhythm. The conference, which had brought 92,000 participants, including 4,000 journalists, to the Mediterranean coast, was winding down. Exhibition stands were being dismantled, journalists were leaving their workstations, and delegations were checking out of hotels. The trams kept running, carrying ordinary passengers alongside the last visitors wearing conference badges. In Kaleiçi, restaurants prepared for another evening, and the old harbour stayed busy with tourists.

The next climate conference is scheduled for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in 2027. Its organisers will inherit the unresolved arguments of Antalya and the expectations of countries already experiencing the consequences of climate change. Kumi Naidoo, president of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, had suggested that much of the COP process could be conducted virtually. “I think it would be great if it were a Zoom call,” he said, questioning the need to bring so many people together every year.

Ümit Şahin, climate change studies coordinator at the Istanbul Policy Center, disagreed. “It’s important for the crowd to be here,” he said, pointing to the pressure exerted by civil society and smaller countries. “Without that public pressure, there’s little incentive to act.”
Iftikhar Gilani is an Indian journalist based in Ankara.
